title: Dark Screens: The Pandemic and the Movies

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Part 08: From 2020 to today. Chapter 1: Dark Screens: The Pandemic and the Movies.
segments.text: Part zero eight: From twenty twenty to today. Chapter one: Dark Screens: The Pandemic and the Movies.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In March 2020, COVID-19 shut down movie theaters across the entire planet. Amid postponements, drive-ins and the war over release windows, the way films are released would never be the same.
segments.text: In March twenty twenty, COVID-nineteen shut down movie theaters across the entire planet. Amid postponements, drive-ins and the war over release windows, the way films are released would never be the same.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 2020s began with a celebration. On February 9, Parasite (2019) won the Oscar for Best Picture, the first ever for a non-English-language film, and cinema seemed more global and more alive than ever. A month later, the world stopped. On March 11, the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic. China had already closed some 70,000 screens on January 23, the eve of the Lunar New Year, the most lucrative time of year for the country's theaters. Italy, France, Spain, the United States and Brazil followed within days. By mid-March, the two biggest American chains, AMC and Regal, had closed all their theaters. In more than a century of history, never had so many screens gone dark at the same time.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The first warning came even before the WHO's declaration. On March 4, the producers of No Time to Die (2021), Daniel Craig's farewell as James Bond, pushed its release from April to November 2020: it was the first major film to change dates because of the virus, and it would not be Bond's last delay. In Brazil, 577 screens had already gone dark by March 17. That same week, distributors canceled their releases, and on Thursday, March 19, for the first time in history, not a single film opened in the country's theaters. Cinemark, Kinoplex, Cinépolis, UCI and Espaço Itaú, Brazil's main theater chains, closed their doors with no date to reopen. According to Ancine, Brazil's national film agency, the country's moviegoing audience, which had reached 177.7 million admissions in 2019, plunged to 39.4 million in 2020.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Festivals had to reinvent themselves. The Cannes Film Festival, scheduled for May, at first tried to postpone its edition while part of the Palais des Festivals served as a temporary shelter for homeless people. In April, it admitted it would not take place “in its original form” and ended up announcing a selection under the Cannes 2020 label, with no competition and no Palme d'Or, something that had not happened since 1968. The Venice Film Festival was the first of the major festivals to return in person, from September 2 to 12, with mandatory masks, an empty seat between every two spectators, temperature checks at the entrance and a red carpet with no crowds. The Golden Lion went to Nomadland (2020), by Chloé Zhao. The film premiered on the same day in Venice, in Toronto and at a drive-in set up in the parking lot of the Rose Bowl stadium in California.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Rose Bowl drive-in was not an isolated stopgap. With indoor theaters closed, a format that had seemed like a museum piece was back in fashion. In the United States, open-air theaters, where each family watches the movie from inside its own car, stayed open and became a hot ticket. In Brazil, the Cine Drive-in Brasília, opened in 1973 and one of the last survivors of its kind in the country, reopened on the May 1 holiday in 2020 at half capacity and sold 2,800 tickets that first weekend. In São Paulo, the Petra Belas Artes art house set up a 100-car drive-in at the Memorial da América Latina starting June 16, programming classics by Nolan and Stanley Kubrick. Similar initiatives sprang up in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais and in many other countries. The drive-in saved no one financially, but it became the symbol of an audience that wanted, by any means necessary, to watch movies together.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Amid the chaos, one filmmaker became the spokesman for the movie theater. Christopher Nolan wanted Tenet (2020), starring John David Washington, to be Hollywood's first major release after the shutdown, and he persuaded Warner Bros. not to send it to streaming. Originally set for July 17, the film was pushed to July 31, then to August 12, and finally opened on August 26, 2020, in 70 countries. It reached the United States on September 3, with theaters in New York and Los Angeles still closed. It grossed about US$ 365 million worldwide, only some US$ 58 million of it in the domestic market. Given the circumstances, it was not a flop, but it was not the rescue exhibitors had hoped for either. The studios pushed most of the big releases left on the 2020 calendar into the following year.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The year's tally was brutal. According to the Motion Picture Association, the global box office fell 72% in 2020, closing at US$ 12 billion, compared with more than US$ 40 billion the year before. In the United States and Canada, the drop was 80%. China, which reopened its theaters in July, grossed US$ 3 billion and, for the first time, overtook North America as the world's largest film market. In October, when Bond was delayed again, the chief executive of the British chain Cineworld, owner of Regal, called the decision “the final straw” and indefinitely closed all of its theaters in the U.S., the United Kingdom and Ireland, affecting 45,000 workers. In April 2021, the ArcLight and Pacific chains announced they would not reopen any of their locations, not even the historic Cinerama Dome in Hollywood. Cineworld would file for bankruptcy protection in September 2022, with debts of more than US$ 4.8 billion.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The first battle of the window wars was fought by colorful dolls. With theaters closed, Universal released Trolls World Tour (2020) on April 10, 2020, straight to digital rental in the United States, at $19.99, and the film brought in close to $100 million in three weeks. Buoyed by the result, NBCUniversal chief Jeff Shell told the Wall Street Journal that he planned to release films in both formats even after theaters reopened. The response came on April 28: AMC, the world's largest theater chain, announced it would no longer show any Universal films. The boycott lasted three months. At the end of July, the two companies made peace with a landmark deal: theatrical exclusivity, which had been about 90 days, dropped to 17, and the chain began receiving a share of digital revenue.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The theatrical window is the period during which a film plays only in theaters before reaching audiences at home, whether on DVD, digital rental or streaming. It's what guarantees theaters' revenue: if a film comes to TV early, fewer people buy tickets. In 2019, the major chains demanded about 90 days of exclusivity. The pandemic brought down that wall in less than a year. In 2020, the deal between Universal and AMC created the 17-day window, or three weekends. Disney tested paid releases on Disney+, and Warner put an entire year of films on streaming the same day they opened in theaters. When exclusivity returned, it was shorter: in March 2021, Warner struck a deal with Cineworld for a 45-day window starting in 2022, and that period became an industry benchmark. In 2026, exhibitors were still negotiating every week: Universal guaranteed a minimum of five weekends in theaters, seven starting in 2027, and Paramount promised a 45-day window for its releases.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Disney chose a different path. Mulan (2020), the $200 million remake directed by Niki Caro, was scheduled for March 2020 and was postponed several times, until the company gave up on U.S. theaters. On September 4, the film premiered on Disney+ through Premier Access: on top of the subscription, viewers paid $29.99 to watch it. In countries without the service, such as China, it went to theaters, but grossed only about $70 million. In October, Disney announced that Soul (2020), by Pete Docter, would go straight to Disney+, at no extra cost, on Christmas Day 2020. The film won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature and would only reach U.S. theaters in January 2024, three and a half years later than planned.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The hardest blow came on December 3, 2020. Warner announced that all 17 of its 2021 films would open the same day in U.S. theaters and on HBO Max, where they would stay for a month, a plan nicknamed Project Popcorn. The model debuted with Wonder Woman 1984 (2020), by Patty Jenkins, on Christmas Day. Many filmmakers were not consulted. Nolan accused the studio of turning its directors into bait to lure subscribers and said the plan made no economic sense. Denis Villeneuve wrote in Variety that Warner might have just killed the Dune (2021) franchise. The film came out in October 2021 in theaters and on streaming at the same time, and even so, the sequel was green-lit.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The most famous revolt, however, came from a star. On July 9, 2021, Black Widow (2021) opened simultaneously in theaters and on Disney+ Premier Access. On July 29, Scarlett Johansson sued Disney: part of her pay depended on the box office, and the simultaneous release, she argued, breached her contract and drained theaters. The company responded publicly that the actress had already been paid $20 million for the film. The case ended in a settlement on September 30, 2021, for an undisclosed amount. It was a watershed: it became clear that streaming was changing not only theaters but also how the people who make films get paid, a debate that would return in force in the 2023 Hollywood strikes.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Even the Oscars changed their look. The 2021 ceremony was pushed back from February 28 to April 25, and for the first time films released only on streaming were eligible, as long as they had a planned theatrical release. The show left the Dolby Theatre and moved to Union Station, the Los Angeles train station, with a reduced audience. Nomadland, a quiet portrait of Americans who have lost their homes and live on the road, won Best Picture, Director and Actress, the last for Frances McDormand, her third Oscar in the category. Chloé Zhao became the second woman to win as director and the first woman of color. But the ceremony drew few viewers, in the hall and at home: with 10.4 million viewers in the U.S., it was the least-watched broadcast since record-keeping began.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The comeback only became clear at the end of 2021, when Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021), starring Tom Holland, opened exclusively in theaters, on December 16 in Brazil and the following day in the United States, and became the first film since the start of the pandemic to top US$ 1 billion. The old world, however, did not come back. The 90-day theatrical window gave way to windows of 17 to 45 days, and in early 2026 projections still put the global box office about 13% below its 2017–2019 average. In Brazil, by 2025, there were already more screens than in 2019, but far fewer moviegoers. It is in this shaken film industry that the rest of the decade begins: social media dictating success, horror as the safe bet, filmmakers coming from YouTube, the strikes and artificial intelligence, the strength of films from outside Hollywood, the streaming wars and the return of the event movie.
